newsitem.title: USA: King estate sues CBS over "Dream" speech tape sales.
newsitem.headline: King estate sues CBS over "Dream" speech tape sales.

text.p: The estate of Martin Luther King Jr. sued CBS Inc. Tuesday over the television network's sale of a videotape cassette featuring the slain civil rights leader's 1963 "I Have a Dream" speech.

In a copyright infringement suit filed in U.S. District Court in Atlanta, the King estate sought unspecified damages against CBS for the "unauthorized and inappropriate" use of copyrighted King property in an episode of the television documentary series, "The 20th Century with Mike Wallace."
Videocassettes from the series, which already has run on the Arts & Entertainment cable TV channel, are available to the public for about $30 apiece.

"CBS is using almost all of the speech without permission or acknowledgment of the King Estate's copyright, and for its own profit. We view this as particularly improper," said Phillip Jones, chief executive of Intellectual Properties Management Inc., an Atlanta firm that manages the King estate.

Meanwhile the network, a subsidiary of Westinghouse Electric Corp., said its use of the speech is protected both by U.S. copyright law and the First Amendment because the documentary consists entirely of CBS news footage.
"CBS News covered the event live," CBS News President Andrew Heyward said in a statement.

"The suggestion that a news organisation must receive permission to use its own footage of one of the most public and newsworthy events of this century cannot be squared with our central responsibility to preserve the free flow of vital political, social and historical information."
King's speech, with its famed "I Have a Dream" refrain, provided the emotional climax for the Civil Rights Movement's "March on Washington" on Aug. 28, 1963.

King delivered the nationally televised address to a crowd of about 250,000 people in front of the Lincoln Memorial at the height of the Civil Rights movement. Six days later he registered it with the U.S. Copyright Office. A month after that, he sued a record company for selling pirated recordings.
The King estate said it tried for months to get CBS to reach an agreement voluntarily.

"It is unfortunate that we are forced to bring this action. We attempted repeatedly to resolve this conflict amicably with no meaningful response. Because of the blatant nature of the infringement, we had no choice," said Jones.
Intellectual Properties Management licensed the same speech for use during the opening ceremonies of last summer's Olympic Games.
"The amount of damages will depend on the profits earned by CBS, the damage to the estate and the court's descretion in determining statutory damages," noted King attorney Joseph Beck.
